Let \(S=X_1+\cdots+X_{10}\). By exchangeability, the law is determined by \(p_s=\mathbb P(S=s)\). Also, independence of every subfamily of size at most \(5\) is equivalent to

\[
\mathbb E\binom Sj=\binom{10}{j}2^{-j},\qquad j=0,1,\dots,5.
\]

Indeed, these are exactly the probabilities that any fixed \(j\) coordinates are all \(1\), and by linearity they determine all pattern probabilities of size \(\le 5\).

Now consider

\[
Q(s)=-\frac{(s-3)(s-4)(s-6)(s-7)(s-10)}{5040}.
\]

For integer \(s=0,1,\dots,10\), this satisfies

\[
Q(0)=1,\qquad Q(s)\ge 0\quad (1\le s\le 10).
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{s=0\}}\le Q(s),
\]

so for every admissible law,

\[
p_0\le \mathbb E Q(S).
\]

Since \(Q\) has degree \(5\), \(\mathbb E Q(S)\) is fixed by the five-wise independence moments, so it equals its value for \(B\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,1/2)\). Expanding in the binomial basis,

\[
\begin{aligned}
&(s-3)(s-4)(s-6)(s-7)(s-10)\\
&=-5040+3420\binom s1-2120\binom s2+1140\binom s3-480\binom s4+120\binom s5.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb E Q(S)
=
-\frac1{5040}
\left(
-5040+3420\cdot 5-2120\cdot \frac{45}{4}
+1140\cdot 15-480\cdot \frac{210}{16}
+120\cdot \frac{252}{32}
\right)
=\frac1{112}.
\]

So \(p_0\le 1/112\).

Equality forces \(p_s=0\) whenever \(Q(s)>0\), namely for

\[
s=1,2,5,8,9.
\]

Solving the six moment equations on the remaining support \(\{0,3,4,6,7,10\}\) gives

\[
p_0=p_{10}=\frac1{112},\qquad
p_3=p_7=\frac5{28},\qquad
p_4=p_6=\frac5{16},
\]

and all other \(p_s\) are \(0\). This law is feasible: its generating function differs from the binomial generating function by

\[
\sum_{s=0}^{10}p_s z^s-\left(\frac{1+z}{2}\right)^{10}
=
\frac{(z-1)^6}{1024\cdot 7}
\left(57+272z+462z^2+272z^3+57z^4\right),
\]

so its first five derivatives at \(z=1\) agree with those of \(\left(\frac{1+z}{2}\right)^{10}\).

Therefore the maximizing distribution vector is

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\frac1{112},\,0,\,0,\,\frac5{28},\,\frac5{16},\,0,\,
\frac5{16},\,\frac5{28},\,0,\,0,\,\frac1{112}
\right)
}.
\]
